description: We are Team Girl Power, passionate about space and technology, and we are looking for enthusiastic developers and designers to build a great project together.
summary:
We developed Earth Jukebox, a sonification system that makes NASA Earth science data accessible through sound, voice and touch instead of sight alone.

NASA shares much of its Earth data as colour maps and animations, which blind and low-vision people cannot use and many others find hard to interpret. Our system lets a person explore these data by pointing. A hand landmark detection model tracks the fingers, and the pointed location is converted into geographic coordinates and the data value there. It works in two ways. In the virtual mode only a camera is needed: a map or globe is drawn over the live camera picture, and the user points at it, zooms the map or turns the globe with hand gestures. In the physical mode the camera recognises a printed world map or a real globe; the system fits the map's projection and follows the globe's 3D position, so the object can be moved and spun while pointing. Values become pitch, rhythm and recorded sounds, and a voise assistant helpl through the proces and describes the place, date and value.

The result is a low-cost, offline tool that opens NASA's open data to people who cannot see it and gives everyone a more intuitive way to understand our changing planet.
details:
PROBLEM

NASA shares a large part of its Earth science as colour maps and animations. They are rich, but they rely on sight alone: a blind or low-vision person cannot read them, and for many sighted people a colour legend still says little about what the numbers mean. Our goal was to make the same data understandable through sound, voice and touch, using objects people already know: a map and a globe.

OUR SOLUTION

A camera watches the user's hands and a surface: a printed world map, a physical globe, or a virtual map or globe drawn over the camera picture. The user points with the right index finger and hears the value of the selected dataset at that place in real time. The left hand moves through time, rotates the globe or zooms the map. When the finger stays still for three seconds, a voice describes the place, the date, the value and how it compares with the long-term normal.

HOW IT WORKS

Hand tracking. A hand landmark detection model (Google MediaPipe Hand Landmarker) finds 21 keypoints on each hand in every frame. The index fingertip is used for pointing, and the thumb and index positions for pinch and zoom gestures.

From pixel to coordinates. For a paper map, the sheet is located in the frame with ORB features and a homography. The map projection (equirectangular, Mercator, Miller or Robinson) is fitted from a few known landmarks, so any printed map can be used. For a physical globe, the system builds a memory of the globe's surface during calibration and estimates its 3D pose in every frame (PnP), so the globe can be spun, moved and tilted. Virtual surfaces use ray-sphere intersection and map projection directly.

From data to sound. The value under the finger is mapped to a pentatonic note (C3 to E5), which keeps every combination pleasant to hear. The difference from the baseline adds beating and a pulse, so warming is heard as rising tension, and longitude sets the stereo position. Instead of notes, a dataset can be given recorded sounds. Several loops play at once and the value controls their mix with constant loudness (gain = square root of the share). Ocean current speed, for example, moves from a calm river to a roaring sea. Earthquake data can also be felt as vibration of the laptop trackpad.

Speech. Place names come offline from Natural Earth outlines (country, sea, region). The sentence is spoken by Kokoro-82M, a neural text-to-speech model that runs locally.

OPEN TO NEW DATA AND NEW SOUNDS

Much of NASA's data reaches the public as videos from the Scientific Visualization Studio. Earth Jukebox can convert such a video into a data layer. It detects the colour bar and the map area, matches every pixel to the scale in perceptual (Lab) colour space, ignores text and coastlines, and turns frames into time steps. As a demonstration we converted the SVS animation of PM2.5 air pollution from NASA's GEOS-CF model (https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/5151/). NetCDF files are supported as well.

Users can also give any map its own sound without coding. Two recordings, for example light and strong wind, are enough: the program mixes them in proportion to the value, turning a gradient map into a gradient of sound. Up to eight recordings can be used for finer steps.

IMPACT

Earth Jukebox makes global climate data accessible to blind and low-vision people, and gives every learner a physical way to understand it: one slide of a finger across a map plays 145 years of warming. It needs only a laptop camera (or a phone) and any printed map or globe, works offline, and lets teachers, museums and communities add new NASA visualizations and their own sounds in minutes.

TOOLS

Python, MediaPipe Hand Landmarker, OpenCV, NumPy, SciPy, xarray, h5netcdf, sounddevice, Kokoro-82M text-to-speech, Natural Earth. Hardware: MacBook, webcam or iPhone as a camera, a printed world map and a globe.
